heard: Can you measure the whole earth with a stick? By the end of this, you'll know exactly how one man did it 2 ,200 years ago, where his number went wrong and how you can do it yourself with a friend and a ruler. Here's the problem. You live in Alexandria and Egypt, around 240 BC. You want to know how big the earth is. You can't walk around it, and you can't fly above it. What you can do is watch the sun. Far to the south is a town called Saidine, today's ass one. On the longest day of the year, at noon, the sun shines straight down a well there. No shadow at all. On the same day, at the same noon, stand a stick up in Alexandria. It does cast a shadow. Measure the angle between the stick and the sun's ray, about 7 .2 degrees. Now the key step. 7 .2 degrees is 150th of a full circle. So the distance from Saidine to Alexandria is 150th of the way around the earth. Pay someone to pace the distance. The number that comes back is 5 ,000 stadia. Multiply by 50, the earth is 250 ,000 stadia around. The man who did this was Eratosthenes, the head of the great library of Alexandria. His rivals nicknamed him beta, number two, because he was never the best at any one thing. He measured the planet anyway. So why should a shadow in one city tell you the size of the whole earth? Draw it. Here's the earth, cut in half through both cities. At Saidine, the sun's ray goes straight down the well. Extend that line, and it passes through the center of the earth. At Alexandria, the stick also points to the center of the earth. That's what standing straight up means on a ball. Now the sun's rays. The sun is so far away that the ray hitting Saidine and the ray hitting Alexandria are parallel. Two parallel lines, crossed by the sticks line. The angle at the top, between the stick and the ray, equals the angle at the center, between the two cities. It's the same angle you learned about in school, where a line crosses two parallel lines. So the shadow angle is the slice of the earth between the cities. A 7 .2 degrees slice, 50 of them to go around. How parallel is parallel? The sun is about 150 million kilometers away. The two cities are about 800 kilometers apart. The two rays differ by about 3 -10 thousandths of a degree. Nothing a stick could ever see. That's the first answer. If you like seeing the math hiding behind everyday things, subscribe. There's a new one twice a day. But here's a catch most retelling skip. Two sticks can't prove the earth is round. Imagine the earth is flat, and the sun is close, hanging about 6 ,300 kilometers above Saidine. Then the stick in Saidine casts no shadow, and the stick in Alexandria 800 kilometers away leans away from the sun by 7 .2 degrees. Exactly the same shadows. Eratosthenes didn't need to prove the earth was round. Greek thinkers had said so since the 5th century BC, and the earth's round shadow on the moon in an eclipse backs them up. He took the ball as given and measured it. If you did want to tell the two apart, you'd need a third stick. Far away. On a ball, a stick 5 ,000 kilometers north of the well leans 45 degrees. Under a close sun over a flat earth, it leans only 38. The further you go, the wider the gap. So how good was his number? It depends on three things, and all three are shaky. First, the distance. 5 ,000 is suspiciously round. Pacers called bemedists, walked roots, and counted steps. Their number was probably rounded, maybe even to fit the 150th. Second, the geometry. Syene isn't exactly where the sun is straight overhead on the longest day. It's a little north of that line, and it isn't due south of Alexandria. It's about three degrees east. Here's the lucky part. Using modern maps, the two cities are 7 .1 degrees of latitude apart, not 7 .2, and about 790 kilometers apart from north to south. The errors pull in opposite directions and mostly cancel. Third and worst, nobody is sure how long the stadium was. Greek cities use different ones, from about 160 meters to 210. Take the short one, 160 meters, and 250 ,000 stadia is 40 ,000 kilometers. The real distance around the poles, 40 ,000 eight. Take 185 meters, and you get 46 ,000, 250, 16 % too big. Take 210, and you get 52 ,500. So, the method was perfect and the number is somewhere between nearly exact and almost a third too large. Historians still argue which. In 2012, someone repeated the experiment with modern tools and got 40 ,000 in 74 kilometers, within 66 kilometers of the real thing. The method works. The next person to try did worse, and it mattered. Around 100 years later, Posadonius used a star instead of the sun. A bright star called Canopus just grazes the horizon at roads, but rises 7 .5 degrees high in Alexandria. 7 .5 degrees is 148th of a circle. He took roads to be 5 ,000 stadia from Alexandria and got 240 ,000 stadia, close to Eratostens. But the distance across the sea was hard to know. Another version used 3 ,750 stadia instead. Times 48, that's only 180 ,000. That small earth stuck. The astronomer Ptolemy used 180 ,000, and his maps were copied for over a thousand years. His earth was about a third too small. Columbus used a small earth like that to argue Asia was a short sail west. It wasn't. He was saved only by a continent nobody in Europe knew was there. Same method, same kind of angle. One bad distance, and the planet shrank by a third. Measuring the earth wasn't even his day job. Remember the nickname Beta number two. Here's what number two also did. He drew a map of the known world on a grid of lines running east to west and north to south, and placed over 400 cities on it. He coined the word geography. He worked out a calendar of 365 days with an extra day every fourth year. The same rule Julius Caesar's calendar used two centuries later, and his name is still on a way to list prime numbers, the sieve of Eratosthenes. Write the numbers up to 30. Cross out every multiple of two after two, then of three, then of five. What's left are the 10 primes below 30. Not bad for number two. Here's where the story loops back on itself. In the 1790s, France wanted a unit of length that belonged to nobody, so they took it from the earth itself. Two astronomers, Delombra and Michae, surveyed the line from Dunkirk to Barcelona. The meter would be one 10 millionth of the distance from the north pole to the equator. A quarter of the way around is 10 million meters. So the whole way around is 40 million meters, 40 ,000 kilometers, by definition. Their first meter bar came out a fifth of a millimeter short. That's why the real number today is 40 ,000 eight, not exactly 40 ,000. So when Eratosthenes' short stadium gives 40 ,000 kilometers, it's lining up with a unit that was built from the same planet he measured. Now your turn. You don't need a well, and you don't need the longest day. You need two places, one roughly north of the other, and two people who measure a noon shadow on the same day. Stand a one meter stick up straight. At noon, when the shadow is shortest, measure the shadow. The angle comes from the ratio of shadow to stick. Say the stick is one meter, and the shadow is half a meter. Then the sun is about 26 .6 degrees away from straight up. A handy check. On the spring or autumn equinox, at 45 degrees north, a one meter stick casts a shadow almost exactly one meter long. Your friend measures two. Subtract the two angles. That difference is your slice of the earth. With a friend 1 ,000 kilometers south, your shadows differ by about nine degrees. Nine degrees is one -fortieth of a circle. 1 ,000 times 40 -40 ,000 kilometers. Schools around the world do exactly this every equinox, comparing shadows by email. A ruler, a stick, and a friend are enough. So, to sum up. The sun's rays arrive parallel. A stick points to the center of the earth, so a shadow angle is a slice of the planet. Measure the slice. Measure the distance. Multiply. Eratosthenes did it with a well, a stick, and a hired walker. His method was perfect, his units are still argued over, and a worst copy of his idea sent Columbus the wrong way. Here's one to check. You and a friend measure noon shadows on the same day, and your angles differ by 3 .6 degrees. How far apart are you? Answer in the comments.
chapters: 4:51 A wrong number that changed history
